701.title: Garuda and the nectar
701.hook: Garuda steals the nectar of the gods to buy his mother's freedom, and never tastes a drop
701.carry: seva: serve without taking a sip
701.tomorrow: why would a king hang a dead snake on a silent sage?
701.howItsDone: In many Vishnu temples, especially in South India, an image of Garuda stands facing the shrine with folded hands, as Vishnu's mount and model servant. Kusha (darbha) grass is used in many Hindu rites, and some families retell Garuda's story to children as a story of loyalty to a mother.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kadru's bet, black hairs on a white horse, and the snake sons who refused to cheat. The nagas are honored, not hated.
screen: `THE NAGAS ARE HONORED, NOT HATED.`

segments.voice: An egg cracks open and something blazing comes out, so bright the gods take it for fire. It's Garuda, Vinata's son, a bird of enormous strength. He grows up to find his mother a slave to her sister, made to carry the snakes wherever they want to go. So he asks the snakes the obvious question: what would it take to set her free? They name a price nobody could pay. Bring us the amrita, the nectar of immortality, which the gods keep for themselves.
screen: `A BLAZING EGG.` → `HIS MOTHER, A SLAVE.` → `THE PRICE: THE GODS' NECTAR.`

segments.voice: So Garuda goes to get it. He fights past the gods and a spinning wheel of blades, and takes the amrita. The first surprise: he doesn't drink it. He could make himself immortal on the spot, and he carries it away untouched, because it's for his mother's freedom. Vishnu is so pleased that he grants Garuda boons: a place on Vishnu's banner, and immortality without a drop of the nectar. Garuda offers a boon in return, and Vishnu asks him to be his mount. Then Indra, king of the gods, asks for the nectar back. Garuda makes him an offer: I've promised it to the snakes, and I'll let no one drink it. But wherever I set it down, you may take it up. Garuda sets the nectar down for the snakes on a bed of kusha grass. My mother is free, he says. Go and bathe before you drink. While they bathe, Indra takes the amrita back to heaven, as agreed. The snakes lick the empty grass, and its sharp blades split their tongues. That, the story says, is why snakes have forked tongues, and why kusha grass is held holy. Now the teaching Hindus keep from it. The one who held immortality in his claws and didn't take a sip is the one Vishnu chose to carry him. That's seva, service, at the heart of bhakti: you carry what's precious, and you don't help yourself along the way. In many Vishnu temples, Garuda stands before the shrine with folded hands, facing his Lord.

702.title: Parikshit's seven nights
702.hook: a tired king drapes a dead snake on a silent sage, and a chain of small choices ends in Takshaka's bite
702.carry: karma is a chain; kshama can break it
702.tomorrow: the fire is lit. who can stop a king's revenge?
702.howItsDone: Vows of silence, mauna, are kept by some Hindu ascetics and by some householders for a day or a season. Parikshit's death is also the setting of the Bhagavata Purana, which tradition says was recited to him in his last days.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Adi Parva: Garuda, the nectar he never tasted, and the bird who became Vishnu's mount. Seva: serve without taking a sip.
screen: `SEVA: SERVE WITHOUT TAKING A SIP.`

segments.voice: A king is out hunting, and he's lost a deer he wounded. He comes on an old sage sitting very still, and asks: did a deer pass this way? The sage says nothing. He's keeping a vow of silence. The king asks again. Nothing. And the king, tired, hungry and stung, lifts a dead snake on the end of his bow and drapes it over the old man's shoulders. Then he rides home. The king is Parikshit, Janamejaya's father. The sage is Shamika. This is how Janamejaya's wound was made.
screen: `A LOST DEER, A SILENT SAGE.` → `A DEAD SNAKE ON HIS SHOULDERS.` → `JANAMEJAYA'S WOUND.`

segments.voice: Shamika doesn't move. He bears it. But his son Shringin, a young man with a hot temper and real power from his austerities, hears about it, and curses the king: within seven nights, Takshaka, king of the snakes, will bite him, and he will die. Now watch the father. Shamika is not pleased. Forgiveness, kshama, is a sage's strength, he tells his son, and the king protects people like us. He sends a disciple to warn Parikshit. The king takes the warning seriously. He builds a palace on a single pillar and fills it with guards and healers. A sage named Kashyapa, who can cure snakebite, sets out to save him. Takshaka meets him on the road and pays him to go home, and Kashyapa turns back. Then snakes come disguised as ascetics, carrying fruit for the king. In one fruit is a tiny insect. As the sun goes down on the seventh day, Parikshit, thinking the danger has passed, picks it up and says, half in jest: let this one bite me. The insect becomes Takshaka, and the king dies. Look at the chain. A sage's silence. A king's insult. A son's curse. A healer paid off. A joke at sunset. Hindus call this karma: every act bears fruit, and the fruit of one act becomes the seed of the next. Many teachers read karma this way, as a web of many people's acts, not one quick verdict on one person. And notice the only one who tried to stop the chain: the old sage, who answered harm with kshama. His son didn't listen. That's the frame Janamejaya stands in, and his fire is the next link.
screen: `A SON'S CURSE: SEVEN NIGHTS.` · `THE FATHER: FORGIVENESS IS STRENGTH.` · `A HEALER PAID TO TURN BACK.` · `TAKSHAKA HIDDEN IN A FRUIT.` · then, large: `KARMA IS A CHAIN; KSHAMA CAN BREAK IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small, sharp thing someone did to you lately: a word, a look, a joke at your expense. Notice the next link you'd like to add. 703.title: Astika stops the fire
703.hook: a young sage, half from the snakes' own family, asks the king for one gift: stop the fire
703.carry: listening to the sacred story is itself devotion
703.tomorrow: what did a king in heaven do to get sent back down?
703.howItsDone: Many Hindu families and temples hold katha: a sacred story, such as the Mahabharata, the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana, told or recited aloud, sometimes over many evenings, and hearing it is held to be devotion in itself. In some households Astika's name is remembered as a protection against snakes, in keeping with the promise the story records.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: a dead snake on a silent sage, a son's curse, and Takshaka hidden in a fruit. Karma is a chain; kshama can break it.
screen: `KARMA IS A CHAIN; KSHAMA CAN BREAK IT.`

segments.voice: The fire is lit. Janamejaya has heard how his father died, and his priests begin the snake sacrifice. As they chant, snakes are drawn from everywhere into the flames, the text says, great and small, crying out as they fall. Takshaka, the one the king most wants, has fled to Indra for protection. And a young man is walking toward the sacrifice, sent by his mother. His name is Astika. His father is a sage, his mother is the sister of a snake king, and he has come to stop the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE IS LIT.` → `TAKSHAKA HIDES WITH INDRA.` → `A YOUNG SAGE IS COMING.`

segments.voice: Astika's story starts with his father, a sage named Jaratkaru, who wanted no wife and no home. One day he found his ancestors hanging head down over a pit, holding a thin root that a rat was gnawing. They were falling, they told him, because their line would end with him. So Jaratkaru agreed to marry, on strange terms: only a bride who shared his name. The snake king Vasuki had a sister named Jaratkaru, and he'd been told a child of this marriage would save the snakes. That child is Astika. At the sacrifice, Astika doesn't argue or threaten. He praises the king, the priests and the fire, so well that Janamejaya wants to give him a gift. Ask for anything, the king says. And Astika asks: stop the sacrifice. The king offers other gifts. Astika holds to his one request. By now Takshaka is falling toward the flames, held in the air above them. The assembly urges the king to keep his word, and Janamejaya does. The fire stops. Takshaka is spared. And at this sacrifice, the text says, Vaishampayana tells the king his family's great story. So the frame closes on a king who came to burn and stayed to listen. Hindus call that shravana, hearing, and the Bhagavata Purana names it first among the ways of devotion. That's why families still gather for katha, a sacred story told aloud over many evenings, and why the Mahabharata itself promises good to those who hear it. On the first day of this year we met him beside a fire. We leave him listening.

segments.voice: For two minutes, just listen, without planning what you'll say back: to someone at home telling you about their day, to a recorded bhajan or chant, or to a few lines of a sacred text read aloud. When your mind starts drafting a reply, set it down and go back to hearing. Janamejaya came to burn, and stayed to listen.

704.title: The king who looked too long
704.hook: a king in heaven stares too long at the river goddess, and gods under a curse ask her for a terrible favor
704.carry: karma carries into the next birth
704.tomorrow: a woman rises from a river. whose wife will she be?
704.howItsDone: At the Ganga, the river is honored as a goddess: pilgrims bathe in her waters, some carry Ganga water home in sealed vessels, and lamps are offered to her at evening aarti on her banks.

screen: `DAY SEVEN-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Astika asked, the fire stopped, and Janamejaya sat down to hear the story. Listening to the sacred story is itself devotion.

segments.voice: A court in heaven. The gods are gathered before Brahma, and among them is a king, Mahabhisha, who earned his place there by his deeds on earth. Then the river goddess Ganga arrives. A wind lifts her garment. The gods lower their eyes. Mahabhisha doesn't. He looks, and keeps looking. Brahma sees it, and tells him: you will be born again among mortals. This part of the Kuru story starts with a stare.
screen: `A COURT IN HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS LOWER THEIR EYES.` → `ONE KING KEEPS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: The text sets it up with two curses, side by side. The first is Mahabhisha's. Brahma sends him down to be born on earth, and tells him that Ganga, the one who stole his mind, will cross him there, and that his time on earth will end when he finally loses his temper with her. Mahabhisha chooses to be born as the son of a good king named Pratipa. The second curse belongs to the Vasus, a group of gods. On her way back, Ganga meets them, downcast. The sage Vasishtha has cursed them to be born as men, and they don't want to linger in human lives. So they ask a strange favor: be our mother on earth, and as each of us is born, throw us into your waters, so we're set free at once. Ganga agrees, with one condition: one son has to live. Each Vasu gives a portion of his power to that son, who will live long and, they say, have no children. Hold that detail. Now look at what this story takes for granted, because Hindus do too. A king can earn heaven by his deeds and still be born again. Gods can be born as men. This is samsara, the round of births, and karma is what turns it: what you do, even where you let your eyes rest, carries into the next birth. Even heaven isn't the end. That's why the Vasus don't ask for long lives; they ask for release. Hindus call that release moksha, and we'll watch Ganga give it.

You sat on the right, so you'll be my son's wife.

segments.voice: The woman is Ganga, and she agrees: she'll marry Pratipa's son, on one condition, that whatever she does, he won't question it. A son is born: Shantanu, who is Mahabhisha come down from heaven. When Shantanu is grown, Pratipa hands him the kingdom, and a message with it. A lovely woman may come to you. If she does, take her as your wife. Don't ask who she is, and don't question what she does. One day, walking along the bank of the Ganga, Shantanu sees a woman by the water, and he's struck. He asks her to be his wife. She answers with terms. Whatever I do, good or bad, you must never stop me or speak harshly to me. The moment you do, I'll leave. He agrees. Now notice what we know that he doesn't: she's Ganga, and she's promised the Vasus. He knows only that he's in love, and that he's given his word. In this epic, a given word is never small talk. Keeping it is dharma, and the Mahabharata tests that again and again; one vow coming soon will shape the whole Kuru line. Hindus still make their biggest promises out loud and witnessed. At a wedding, the couple circles the sacred fire and takes seven steps together, the saptapadi, with Agni, the fire, as witness. Shantanu's vow had no fire and no family, only a riverbank and a man in love, and it will hold his tongue for years. They marry, and the text says they're happy together. And their first child is on the way.

segments.voice: A son is born to the king and queen. And the queen carries the baby down to the river, and gives him to the Ganga's waters. As she does it, she says it's for his good. Shantanu watches from the bank, and says nothing. He remembers what he promised: never stop her, never speak harshly to her, or she leaves. Another son is born, and the same thing happens. And another. The text tells it plainly, without looking away.
screen: `A SON, GIVEN TO THE RIVER.` → `THE KING SAYS NOTHING.` → `ANOTHER SON. AND ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Seven sons, the text says, one after another, into the river. Every time, Shantanu stays silent, afraid that if he speaks, she'll leave him. Then the eighth son is born. As she carries this one toward the river, Shantanu can't hold it in. Don't kill him, he says. Who are you? Why do you kill your own sons? She stops. I won't kill this one, she says. But my time with you is over, as we agreed. And she tells him who she is: Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu, the text says. The sons were the Vasus, cursed to be born as men, and she has freed them as she promised. The scene can be seen more than one way. For Shantanu, these were his children, lost in front of him. For the Vasus, it was the release they begged for. The Mahabharata doesn't smooth this over; it lets the scene stay hard. But look at what the Vasus asked for: not more life on earth, but to be set free from a human birth, and Ganga's waters did it. Hindus hold on to that: her waters free and purify. The deepest freedom Hindus seek is moksha, release from the round of births itself, and for many, the Ganga is bound up with that hope. That's why families carry the ashes of their dead to her at Haridwar and Varanasi, and why a few drops of Ganga water may be placed on the lips of the dying. The son who lives carries the Vasus' power, and their word that he'll have no children. Ganga takes the child with her, and goes.

segments.voice: His wife has just told Shantanu she is Ganga, and that his seven lost sons were the Vasus, gods under a curse. His promise is broken, and she's about to go. So he asks the one thing he still can: what did the Vasus do, that they had to be born as men and die as babies? Ganga answers him before she leaves. Her answer starts on a mountainside, with a sage and his cow.
screen: `WHAT DID THEY DO?` → `GANGA ANSWERS BEFORE SHE GOES.` → `A SAGE AND HIS COW.`

segments.voice: The sage is Vasishtha. He keeps his hermitage on a mountain slope, and he owns a wondrous cow named Nandini, one of the wish-giving cows of Hindu story. One day the Vasus come wandering there with their wives. One wife sees the cow and wants her, not for herself, but for a friend on earth, a princess, so her friend might stay young and free of illness. Her husband is a Vasu named Dyu. He knows whose cow this is. But to please his wife, with his brothers helping, he takes her. Vasishtha comes back to an empty pasture, sees with a sage's inner sight what happened, and curses the Vasus: they will be born on earth as men. The Vasus beg him to take it back. He can't unsay the curse. But he can shape what follows. The seven who helped will be freed soon after they're born. Dyu, who took the cow, will live a long life on earth: virtuous and learned, devoted to his father, and with no children. So the eighth son, the one Shantanu saved by speaking, is Dyu himself. Two teachings sit in this. The first is why the story turns on a cow. In Hindu tradition the cow is honored as a giver, gau mata, mother cow: like a mother, she feeds others and asks little. To rob a sage of his cow was a grave wrong, grave enough to bring gods down to earth. The second is karma, measured to fit: the helpers are freed fast, and the one who took the cow carries the longest life.
